Guides

Performance

Why routiva stays fast — compiled routes, a linear dispatch scan, streaming I/O — and how to benchmark your own workload.

Fast because it is small#

routiva does not quote a throughput number, because a number from one machine does not transfer to another. It is quick for a concrete reason: it does little per request. There is no dependency graph to load, no routing table rebuilt on each call, no body buffered that could be streamed, and no compression performed unless the client asked for it.

This page describes the cost model so you can reason about your own app, then shows how to measure it.

Where the time goes#

A request touches four things:

  1. Wrap. new Request(raw) parses the URL, query string and cookies once.
  2. Dispatch. The layer stack is scanned until a layer matches and responds.
  3. Handler. Your code runs.
  4. Serialize. res.send() writes headers and a body.

The framework owns steps 1, 2 and 4. Step 2 grows with the number of layers, so the design keeps that scan cheap and predictable.

Routes compile once#

Patterns become a RegExp at registration time, never per request. compile(pattern, end) in src/router.js:

text
/users/:id    ->  /^\/users\/([^/]+)\/?$/    keys: ['id']
/files/*      ->  /^\/files\/(.*)\/?$/       keys: ['wildcard']
/api (mount)  ->  /^\/api(?=\/|$)/           prefix, not anchored to the end

Literal segments are regex-escaped, :name becomes ([^/]+) and * becomes (.*). The compiled regex and its keys array are stored on the layer and shared by every request. Dispatch only calls layer.regex.exec(req.path).

The dispatch loop is a linear scan#

All routing runs through one function with a shared cursor:

js
function dispatch(stack, req, res, done) {
  let index = 0;
  let finished = false;

  function next(err) {
    if (finished) return;
    const wantsError = Boolean(err);

    while (index < stack.length) {
      const layer = stack[index++];
      if (layer.isErrorHandler !== wantsError) continue;
      const match = layer.regex.exec(req.path);
      if (!match) continue;
      // ...method check, then invoke(layer, match, err, req, res, next)
      break;
    }
    // stack exhausted -> done(err)
  }

  next();
}

Two properties matter:

  • next() is O(1), not recursive. The cursor never moves backwards, so a chain of next() calls does not re-scan earlier layers or grow the call stack.
  • Error handlers are skipped for free. During normal flow, four-arity layers are filtered out by a single comparison before the regex is even run.

Cost is linear in the number of layers that precede the match.

Per-request allocation#

The only objects created per request are the two wrappers and the small values they hold:

  • new Request(raw) reads raw.url with the URL constructor once, then splits query and cookies into plain objects.
  • new Response(raw, req) stores two references and an empty locals object.
  • During dispatch, invoke() merges params into a fresh object and saves the previous values so a mounted router can restore them on next().

Nothing clones the stack, and no layer is recompiled.

Compression costs CPU to save bytes#

compress() wraps res.send() and decides per response:

text
Accept-Encoding: br, gzip  -> pick br, else gzip, else deflate
body below threshold       -> send as-is
Content-Type not text-ish  -> send as-is
already encoded / streamed -> send as-is

The trade is explicit: brotli and gzip burn CPU and latency to shrink a body. The default threshold is 1kb, so small responses skip the work entirely. A response the client cannot benefit from (already encoded, an image, a streamed file) is left alone. If compression shows up in a profile, raise threshold, pin level, or gate it with filter(req, res).

Because routiva buffers res.send() before compressing, it never wraps a file stream. That keeps sendFile streaming, but large generated bodies are compressed in memory.

Static files are cheap when cached#

send.js stats the file, then:

  • sets ETag (W/"size-mtime") and Last-Modified;
  • returns 304 immediately when If-None-Match or If-Modified-Since says the client copy is fresh;
  • sets Cache-Control from maxAge and immutable when configured;
  • serves a single Range as 206 by streaming only that slice.

The 304 path is the win: no body, no read of the file contents. Set a long maxAge for immutable assets and let conditional requests do the rest. The stat call itself is a filesystem hit per request; that is the floor for this strategy.

The rate limit store is a Map#

MemoryStore is a fixed-window counter keyed by IP:

  • hit(key) is one Map lookup and an increment;
  • expired keys are swept by an interval timer created with .unref(), so the timer never keeps the process alive;
  • reset() clears one key or the whole store.

There is no external store. Run more than one process and each keeps its own counters, so a shared limit needs a custom store.

sendFile streams#

pipeFile() uses createReadStream(path, range).pipe(res.raw), so memory stays flat regardless of file size. finish and error events resolve a promise, so the surrounding await still sees failures. Byte ranges stream the same way.

Measuring it#

Measure your app on your hardware. autocannon and wrk are both good:

bash
npm install -g autocannon

# start your app in another shell
node server.js

# 10 connections for 10 seconds
autocannon -c 10 -d 10 http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/products

# 50 connections, JSON POST bodies
autocannon -c 50 -d 20 -m POST \
  -H "content-type=application/json" \
  -b '{"name":"widget","sku":"W-1","price":1}' \
  http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/products

wrk in the same shape:

bash
wrk -t4 -c100 -d30s http://127.0.0.1:3000/health
wrk -t4 -c100 -d30s -s post.lua http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/products

Watch the shape, not just requests per second:

SignalWhat it tells you
requests per secondthroughput at a given concurrency
latency p99tail behaviour under load
CPU per requestheadroom left for middleware
RSS and heapallocation churn and leaks

Compare against a real Express build of the same app on the same machine. Both sit on node:http and run your handlers, so the difference comes from the framework's per-request work, not the socket.

Practical tips#

  • Register cheap middleware first. Each layer is one regex test; a path-mounted middleware costs nothing on other routes.
  • Gate expensive work by path, not by checking inside a global handler.
  • Set a compression threshold that matches your typical payload.
  • Give static assets a long maxAge and rely on ETag for the rest.
  • Stream large files with serveStatic or res.sendFile, not by reading them into a Buffer.
  • Measure before optimizing. Add logger() and read the duration field, or run autocannon. Do not guess.
